theme: Doctrinal Pause: The Return of Christ
summary: Christ’s bodily, visible, personal return; the parousia and its certainty
readingInstruction: Read 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18, Matthew 24:30-31, and Revelation 1:7. Today is a doctrinal pause on the return of Christ. Notice how Paul comforts grieving believers, and how Jesus and John describe his coming.
settingTheScene: The first Christians lived in expectation of Christ’s return. The Thessalonians, new believers, were distressed because some of their number had died before he returned. Would they miss out? Paul writes to correct their ignorance and to comfort them. The second coming of Christ is one of the most frequently repeated promises of the New Testament, and it shapes how Christians live, pray, grieve, and hope.
observation: “But we do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep, that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13).
“For since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so, through Jesus, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep” (1 Thessalonians 4:14).
“For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God” (1 Thessalonians 4:16).
“Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 4:17).
“Therefore encourage one another with these words” (1 Thessalonians 4:18).
“Then will appear in heaven the sign of the Son of Man” (Matthew 24:30).
“And he will send out his angels with a loud trumpet call, and they will gather his elect from the four winds” (Matthew 24:31).
“Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him” (Revelation 1:7).
doctrinalFocus:
The return of Christ, often called the second coming, is the promise that Jesus will come again, personally, visibly, bodily, and gloriously, at the end of the age, to raise the dead, judge the world, and establish his kingdom in its fullness. The angels said at the ascension, “This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1:11). It is the “blessed hope” of the church (Titus 2:13).

Several features are clear. It will be personal: “the Lord himself will descend.” It will be visible and public: “every eye will see him.” It will be glorious, with a cry of command, the voice of an archangel, and the trumpet of God. It will be sudden: “like a thief in the night.” The timing is unknown: not even the angels or the Son know the day or hour (Matthew 24:36). Therefore we are to be ready and watchful. It will bring the resurrection of believers and the transformation of those still alive. It will bring judgment on the living and the dead, and it will complete salvation: the new creation, the end of death, and God dwelling with his people.

Christians have held different views about the details, especially regarding the “rapture” (being caught up in the air) and the millennium. Some hold that Christ will return before a thousand-year reign (premillennialism), with differing views on whether the church goes through the great tribulation. Others hold that the millennium is the present reign of Christ in heaven and with his church (amillennialism). Others hold that the church will bring about a golden age before his return (postmillennialism). These differences matter less than the shared hope: Christ is coming, visibly, to raise the dead, judge, and make all things new. We should hold such details with humility and avoid date-setting.

The doctrine has practical effects. It comforts the grieving: we will see our loved ones in Christ again. It motivates holiness: “everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure” (1 John 3:3). It encourages mission, because the gospel must be preached to all nations before the end. It also sobers us because judgment is coming. And it makes us watchful and active.
interpretation:
Paul writes, “We do not want you to be uninformed, brothers, about those who are asleep, that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope.” Christians do grieve, but not as those without hope. “For since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so, through Jesus, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep.” The resurrection of Jesus is the guarantee of ours.

Then he explains by “a word from the Lord”: “We who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will not precede those who have fallen asleep. For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God. And the dead in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord.” The picture is of a welcoming party: when a king visited a city, citizens went out to meet him and escort him back in. We rise to meet the Lord and come with him. “Therefore encourage one another with these words.” The doctrine of Christ’s return is meant for comfort.

Jesus himself speaks in Matthew 24 of the sign of the Son of Man appearing in heaven, and all the tribes of the earth mourning as they see the Son of Man coming on the clouds with power and great glory. He will send out his angels with a loud trumpet call, and they will gather his elect from the four winds. This echoes Daniel 7:13-14. For those who have rejected him, his coming means mourning; for his people, it means gathering.

John, in Revelation 1:7, combines Daniel 7:13 and Zechariah 12:10: “Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all tribes of the earth will wail on account of him. Even so. Amen.” The same Jesus who was pierced will return. The right response is to say “Amen” and “Come, Lord Jesus.”
connection: Daniel 7:13-14 and Zechariah 12:10 stand behind the language. Acts 1:9-11 gives the promise at the ascension. Matthew 24:36 to 25:46 includes Jesus’ teaching on being ready. John 14:1-3 promises, “I will come again and take you to myself.” 1 Corinthians 15:51-58 describes the change. Philippians 3:20-21 speaks of our heavenly citizenship. Titus 2:11-14 speaks of the blessed hope. 2 Peter 3:3-13 answers scoffers. Revelation 19:11-16 and 22:20 describe his coming and the church’s cry.
application:
Share verse 18 with someone who is grieving: “Encourage one another with these words.”

Ask whether you live as if Christ may come today. What would you change?

Pray, “Come, Lord Jesus,” as part of your prayers this week.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus that he will return with a shout.
Tell him how you feel about his coming, and ask him to make you ready.
Ask him to give you hope and comfort for those who have died in him.
